title: Mexico Discovers Ceremonial Plaza and Stela of Unknown Culture in Coatepec, Veracruz
author: Ana Mónica Rodríguez
content:
_This article by[Ana Mónica
Rodríguez](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Ana%20M%C3%B3nica%20Rodr%C3%ADguez)
originally appeared in the [August 22, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/08/22/cultura/inah-descubre-
plaza-ceremonial-y-estela-de-cultura-desconocida-en-coatepec-veracruz),
Mexico’s premier left-wing daily newspaper._

In Coatepec, Veracruz, archaeologists from the National Institute of
Anthropology and History (INAH) discovered a civic-ceremonial structure and a
monolithic sculpture with **“characteristics atypical of the region,”** near
the pre-Hispanic zone of Campo Viejo, which is more than 2,000 years old.

What has drawn the specialists’ attention is that it is a platform whose
flanks display circular-shaped stones, and a monolith showing one of two
figures with possible Mayoid features.

In an interview, archaeologists Lino Espinoza García and Alberto Vázquez
Domínguez revealed that, based on the materials found, the settlement of this
civilization “gives us a relative chronology of some 1,500 years before the
Christian era, which is when the settlement of Campo Viejo begins, and from
there on there is a constant population until the colonial period; meanwhile,
the findings of the platform and the stela could have a relative chronology
dating to the Protoclassic period, which ranges between 200 BC and 200 AD.”

They added that **“we are just a few days away from carrying out carbon-14
studies, which could give us an absolute date.”**

![Archaeologists Érika Ramírez and Mireya Moreno at the
excavation](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/2026-08-22-coatepec-
stela-02-archaeologists.jpg)Archaeologists Érika Ramírez and Mireya Moreno.
Photo: INAH

The discovery took place on a private property in the San Lucas subdivision,
where “a platform (30 meters long by 12 meters wide) built with flagstones and
dressed white limestone with a plaster-like texture emerged, a characteristic
achieved by induced means to decorate the walls, possibly through a type of
firing.”

The ornamentation, they explained, consists of lines or figures resembling
squares, and circular-shaped stones on two of its flanks, attributes that are
not characteristic of the region and had not been recorded previously.

A monolithic sculpture was also found, “1.88 meters tall by 1.47 meters wide
at its broadest part, and 68 centimeters at its narrowest. Its thickness
ranges between 22 and 25 centimeters, and it bears engravings alluding to an
event of a symbolic nature in which two elite figures, in a seated position
and with elaborate garments, receive in a vessel a fluid from a divine entity
that is on a higher plane.”

Espinoza García added: “In the stela, two figures are represented in a seated
position, with two vessels in their hands and probably performing a ritual of
petition or initiation; one of them appears to be of advanced age and the
other younger; both wear the same attire (such as headdresses, wristbands,
pectorals, and necklaces), and in the upper part iconographic elements can be
seen alluding to a descending bird, but we are still trying to understand”
each element.

Lino Espinoza noted: “The entire stela, in andesite stone, alludes to matters
of fertility and the cultivation of the land.”

> The entire stela, in andesite stone, alludes to matters of fertility and the
> cultivation of the land.
>
> Lino Espinoza García, INAH archaeologist

Both the structure and the sculpture, which is reminiscent of those of the
Maya culture, were found in a good state of preservation.

During the salvage work, archaeological soundings have been carried out that
have made it possible to recover and identify other pre-Hispanic materials
associated with the structure, “such as remains of charred corn, found in the
form of offerings, vessels, and a green-stone bead fragmented into four parts,
in addition to cinnabar pigments,” which will be sent to the laboratory for
study.

## A Local Civilization

Regarding the culture to which the materials might belong, although the term
Totonac is common for the populations that developed between the Cazones and
Papaloapan rivers, there is a lack of indicators of that civilization at the
site, so the specialists propose that it is a local culture with attributes of
Gulf Coast groups, they indicated.

The field excavations conclude this month, and the specialists will continue
with the laboratory analyses, which will extend into early 2027.

This project, which began at the end of 2025 and was authorized by INAH’s
Archaeology Council, arose from a request for a change in land use for the
development of private urban infrastructure, since the area where the
archaeological work is being carried out, roughly 12 hectares, is intended for
residential use.

The salvage work is also part of the research that the INAH Veracruz Center
has carried out on the periphery of the Campo Viejo archaeological site (where
the San Lucas subdivision is located) since the year 2000, aimed at the
research, protection, and preservation of the archaeological heritage.

Notably, the financial, technological, and specialized-use resources,
professional equipment and tools, as well as support personnel, have been
provided by the property’s owners, who have taken an interest in the
discoveries and their dissemination.
